title: Private Deployments: VPC & On-Prem Deployment Guide, Reference Architectures, Day-2 Ops, and Upgrade/Rollback Procedures
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Summary:
This document consolidates Redwood Inference guidance for private deployments (VPC and on-prem), reference architectures, on-prem packaging options, recommended customer requirements, day-2 operational procedures, and robust upgrade/rollback patterns. It is intended for Solutions Engineering, Platform Engineering, and customer SREs who will deploy or operate Redwood Private.

Scope and audience:
- Scope: deployment topologies (single-region VPC, multi-AZ VPC, air-gapped on-prem), hardware and network requirements, packaging options (helm, OVA, k3s package), day-2 runbooks, upgrade and rollback playbooks, and a customer requirements checklist.
- Audience: customer technical leads, Redwood deploy engineers, platform/on-call SREs.

Overview and key terms:
- Redwood Private: customer-managed control plane and serving runtime deployed inside customer VPC or on-prem environment.
- Day-2 ops: operational tasks after initial install (monitoring, backups, scaling, upgrades).
- Canary rollout: incremental traffic ramp to a new version for safety.

1) Supported deployment modes and recommended use cases
- VPC-managed (recommended for cloud customers): Deploy Redwood Private into a customer AWS/GCP/Azure account using terraform and our helm charts. Best for customers requiring private networking and cloud-managed infrastructure.
- Hybrid VPC + On-Prem: Control plane in customer VPC; inference runtime in on-prem or dedicated colo. Useful for low-latency regional inference with central management.
- On-Prem / Air-gapped: Full stack deployed inside customer firewall with optional HSM/KMS integration. For regulated workloads or customers requiring no egress.

2) Reference architectures (high level)
- Small (Proof of concept)
  - 3 control plane nodes (k8s control plane or managed k8s), 3 worker nodes for runtime; single AZ, limited redundancy.
  - Use case: validation, POC.
- Production (Cloud, multi-AZ)
  - 3 control plane nodes (multi-AZ), autoscaling nodepools for runtime, dedicated GPU nodepools (NVIDIA A100 / H100 or cloud equivalents), separate stateful nodes for object storage and DB.
  - Traffic routing via customer ALB/NGINX ingress, internal service mesh (optional).
- Production (On-Prem / Colo)
  - Multi-rack layout: control plane on management rack (VM or k8s), inference racks with GPU servers, separate storage array for artifacts and KV cache backups, hop-based firewall rules for inter-rack traffic.

Reference architecture table (summary):
| Component | Small | Production (Cloud) | Production (On-Prem) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Control plane nodes | 3 | 3 (multi-AZ) | 3 (HA) |
| Runtime (GPU servers) | 1-2 GPUs | 4+ GPUs per cluster, autoscaling | 8+ GPU servers per inference rack |
| Storage | S3 / local | S3 / regional | Object storage appliance / NFS |
| Networking | Single VPC | Multi-AZ VPC | Private L2/L3 with firewall rules |

3) Minimum customer requirements checklist (pre-deployment)
- Contacts: SRE, network engineer, security/compliance owner, VM provisioning owner.
- Networking:
  - CIDR allocation for control plane and runtime subnets (provide customer terraform variables).
  - Required ports (inbound/outbound) — see ports table below.
  - VPN or Direct Connect (cloud) / Cross-connect (colo) details for remote Redwood support.
- Identity and secrets:
  - KMS/HSM details for customer-managed keys (if required).
  - Service accounts with least privilege for cloud APIs (IAM roles) and SSH keys for node access.
- Compute and Storage:
  - GPU SKU, count, and memory per GPU. Example: 4x NVIDIA A100 80GB per inference node for heavy batching workloads.
  - 1-2 TB NVMe per GPU node for local model cache (adjust per model size).
  - Object storage endpoint and credentials (S3 compatible).
- Observability:
  - Prometheus remote write endpoint or permission to deploy Redwood Prometheus.
  - Log sink (ELK/Datadog) endpoint and API key for log forwarding.
- Compliance:
  - Expected data residency restrictions, audit log retention policy, any required encryption at rest standards.

Network ports (minimum):
| Direction | Port | Purpose | Notes |
|---|---:|---|---:|
| Inbound (from internal) | 443 | API/Control plane | TLS required |
| Inbound | 9090 | Prometheus metrics | Optional if pushing metrics out |
| Inbound | 8600-8700 | Serving runtime gRPC / token streams | Runtime uses ephemeral ports; ensure broad ephemeral range allowed |
| Outbound | 443 | External model download (if allowed) | Block in air-gapped deployments |
| Outbound | 22 | SSH (support) | Use bastion / jump host; prefer restricted CIDR |

4) Packaging options and installation patterns
- Helm (recommended for cloud and connected on-prem)
  - Advantages: repeatable, declarative, integrates with terraform and existing k8s tooling.
  - Typical install command (example):
    - helm repo add redwood https://helm.redwood.ai/charts
    - helm upgrade --install redwood-private redwood/redwood-private -f values-prod.yaml --namespace redwood --create-namespace
  - Values to supply: clusterID, imagePullSecrets, kmsProvider, storage endpoints, gpuSelector labels, nodeAffinity.
- OVA / VM image (for customers needing appliance)
  - Prebuilt OVA contains k3s, runtime container images cached, and offline installer. For air-gapped installs, provide OVA + artifacts bundle.
  - Install steps: import OVA into VMware, power on, run /opt/redwood/install.sh, supply license token and network config.
- k3s / k0s lightweight package (edge/colo)
  - Intended for smaller footprints. We provide a package that includes a bootstrap script to install k3s, CRDs, and Redwood runtime containers.

Packaging security notes:
- All installer artifacts are signed (SHA256 + signature). Verify signatures before install.
- Air-gapped bundle must be ingested to an internal registry and imagePullSecrets configured.

5) Day-2 operations (routine tasks)
- Health checks and monitoring:
  - Verify control plane health: API latency <100ms, control API error rate <0.1% (SLOs).
  - Runtime health: per-host GPU utilization, memory pressure, kubelet restarts.
- Backups and recovery:
  - Backup cadence: daily backups for stateful metadata, hourly snapshots for critical KV caches as configured.
  - Test restore quarterly in a staging environment.
- Scaling operations:
  - Horizontal: add GPU nodes to GPU nodepool; set labels and taints to match runtime affinity.
  - Vertical: increase instance size for high-latency models; ensure GPU memory meets model requirements.
- Log retention and auditing:
  - Retain audit logs for 90 days by default (configurable by customer).
  - Ensure object storage lifecycle policies are in place to avoid runaway cost.
- Common day-2 runbook examples:
  - "High inference latency" – Check model swap events, KV cache hit rate, tail latency on each GPU host, and network egress. If cache miss storm detected, scale runtime or enable prefix caching.
  - "Node OOM or GPU driver crash" – cordon node, drain, restart gpu driver, redeploy runtime pod, and rejoin to cluster. Documented commands: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets; ssh to node -> sudo systemctl restart nvidia-docker; kubectl uncordon <node>.

6) Upgrade strategy and step-by-step playbook
- Principles:
  - Always run upgrades first in a staging environment that mirrors production.
  - Support canary + rollout + automatic rollback on errors.
  - Preserve model cache and KV state during control plane upgrades; runtime upgrades should be graceful with in-flight request draining.

- Pre-upgrade checklist:
  1. Confirm backups: etcd/metadata snapshot, object storage snapshot.
  2. Verify health: all control-plane pods READY, runtime pods in Ready state, SLOs met for 24 hours.
  3. Notify stakeholders and set maintenance window.
  4. Lock config changes (no concurrent deployments).

- Upgrade procedure (recommended canary rollout):
  1. Upgrade control plane components first (API and controllers): helm upgrade redwood-controlplane --namespace redwood -f values-controlplane-upgrade.yaml
  2. Validate control plane: smoke tests (API ping, auth, sample inference) for 10 minutes.
  3. Canary runtime deployment: select 5-10% of GPU capacity (label nodes: redwood-canary=true) and deploy new runtime image to canary nodes.
  4. Route a small percentage of traffic to canary (use ingress rule or traffic routing config). Monitor metrics for 30-60 minutes: latency, error rate, memory growth.
  5. If canary is healthy, gradually increase to 25%, 50%, then 100% with 15-30 minute observation windows.
  6. If any step fails, follow rollback plan (see below).

- Post-upgrade validation:
  - Full e2e tests: model downloads, streaming responses, function calling.
  - Sanity checks for KV cache integrity and local model cache presence.

7) Rollback playbook (fast safe rollback)
- Trigger conditions for rollback:
  - SLO breach exceeding escalation threshold (e.g., p99 latency > 2x baseline for > 10 minutes)
  - Error rate spike > 1% sustained for > 5 minutes
  - Severe node instability (driver crashes, kernel panics)

- Rollback steps (control plane or runtime):
  1. Pause traffic shifts and mark new pods unschedulable.
  2. Redeploy previous stable chart/image with helm rollback or explicit image pin: helm rollback redwood-controlplane <revision> --namespace redwood
  3. For runtime, cordon canary nodes and redeploy older runtime image on them; gradually revert traffic routing.
  4. If data migration was part of upgrade, follow migration revert notes from the migration task (see Appendix B).
  5. Notify stakeholders and open a postmortem tickets.

8) Troubleshooting matrix (common failure modes)
- Problem: Control plane API 503s
  - Likely causes: etcd pressure, leader election flapping, insufficient control-plane CPU.
  - Steps: check etcd metrics, increase control plane replicas temporarily, inspect controller logs (kubectl logs).
- Problem: Serving runtime returns partial responses or broken streams
  - Likely causes: grpc/HTTP/ingress mismatch, resource exhaustion, model load failure.
  - Steps: inspect runtime logs, check model artifact presence on local disk, check kernel OOM logs.

9) Operational playbooks (copyable commands)
- Show control plane status:
  - kubectl get pods -n redwood -o wide
- Cordon and drain GPU node:
  - kubectl cordon gpu-node-01
  - kubectl drain gpu-node-01 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data
- Restart runtime pod with previous image:
  - kubectl -n redwood set image daemonset/redwood-runtime redwood-runtime=myregistry/redwood-runtime:v1.4.2

10) Ownership, escalation, and runbook links
- Primary owner: eng-private-deployments team (pager: #redwood-private-ops)
- Oncall escalation path:
  1. Customer SRE oncall (first 15 minutes)
  2. Redwood private deployments oncall (15-60 minutes)
  3. Redwood platform/serving runtime engineer ( > 60 minutes)
- Useful links:
  - Private deployments playbook: /confluence/eng-private-deployments/private-deployments-playbook-2026
  - Runbooks and incident response: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/runbooks

Appendix A — Example values-prod.yaml (extract)
apiVersion: v1
clusterID: "customer-1234"
imagePullSecrets:
  - name: regcred
kmsProvider:
  provider: "aws-kms"
  keyId: "arn:aws:kms:..."
gpuSelector: "nvidia.com/gpu"

Appendix B — Notes on data migrations (if applicable)
- If an upgrade introduces a schema change in metadata store, a coordinated migration job will run. The migration is reversible only if a rollback path is included in the migration manifest. Always snapshot etcd metadata before running migrations.

Appendix C — Air-gapped install checklist
- Provide full offline bundle (images.tar.gz + charts.tgz + signatures).
- Internal registry and repository path.
- Transport security plan for license tokens and keys.

Document maintenance:
